newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia signals progress on NATO expansion talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia signals progress on NATO expansion talks.

text.p: Russia on Thursday said it had made progress with the West in talks on NATO expansion, signalling the possibility of an agreement ahead of the Western alliance's plans to invite new members in July.

"There has been a certain progress, although we have to say the work is hard, especially on the central question of not bringing the NATO military structure closer to the east," Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told a briefing.

Interfax news agency quoted Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Thursday as telling Russia's Defence Council: "We are ready to discuss concrete initiatives on the part of NATO. Recently such proposals have been appearing."
Russia has for months steadfastly condemned NATO plans to invite former Eastern Bloc nations -- expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- into the alliance.

But a flurry of diplomatic activity in recent weeks appears to have reduced Russian opposition. On Sunday NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana held the third round of talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
"On some questions there has been progress between Russia and NATO, but on other questions there has not been a nearing of positions," Tarasov said.

The public announcement of progress comes two days before Primakov flies to Washington for talks and a week before a scheduled March 19-20 summit between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki.

Tarasov said it was "to soon to say" whether the two leaders might sign an agreement, but said Primakov hoped to narrow differences on the spread of NATO military structure to the east during meetings with Clinton and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
"Russia has some concrete proposals on this score, and Yevgeny Primakov will carry out detailed talks in Washington on the basis of these proposals," Tarasov said.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman said progress in the talks had not come through Russian sacrifices.

"I don't mean that Russia made concessions. I think that we can say that our partners started paying more attention to the concerns Russia has expressed from the beginning regarding NATO expansion," he said.
